column2: On the authority of Abū Saʿīd Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Sinān al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “There is to be no harm and no reciprocating harm.” A ḥasan hadith, reported by Ibn Mājah, al-Dāraquṭnī and others with a connected chain,
and reported by Mālik in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ as mursal, from ʿAmr ibn Yaḥyā, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, omitting Abū Saʿīd. It has routes that strengthen one another.
Lā ḍarar (“no harm”): no one should harm another by depriving him of anything of his right.
Wa-lā ḍirār (“and no reciprocating harm”): he should not inflict harm on his brother when he has suffered no harm [from him], nor repay him with more than the harm he did him.
Harm is to be removed, and many rulings are built on this.
A person is prevented from disposing of his property in a way whose harm extends to others beyond the recognised manner.
Adopting lofty manners and virtuous character towards the children of Ādam.
The noble Prophet ﷺ informs and commands us, for the sake of general welfare, that there is to be no harm and no reciprocating harm; and many contracts and public benefits are built on this.
So every person must not harm his Muslim brother, whether in his person, his wealth or his children,
whether openly or secretly; rather, he should strive to benefit others as long as no harm comes to him from benefiting them.

And whoever suffers harm from someone should not repay him with more than the harm he did him: “And if you punish, then punish with the equivalent of that with which you were harmed” [al-Naḥl 16:126]. If he bears patiently the harm that has befallen him from another

and pardons him, he will find the reward of his patience and pardon with Allah: “But if you are patient, it is better for those who are patient” [al-Naḥl 16:126]; “But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” [al-Shūrā 42:40].
Among what has been said on this:
I will make myself forgive every offence, / however many wrongs are done to me.
People are but one of three: / one above me, one below me, and one my equal who stands against me.
As for the one above me, I recognise his merit / and follow the truth in his regard, for the truth is binding.
As for the one below me, if he speaks [ill], I guard / my honour from answering him, though critics may blame me.
As for the one like me, if he slips or errs, / I am gracious; forbearance is the judge of merit.
